advances: This proves a uniform original-law cubic depth moment for two nonempty four-site coordinate groups with arbitrary second costs, arbitrary ranks, and coordinate-dependent fourth costs. The coefficient is absolute; no ratio bound between the second costs or balance between the ranks is assumed. The argument selects a group of largest rank and applies every mass comparison only within that homogeneous second-cost group at its residual caps. The theorem can also be extended by any number of heterogeneous three-site coordinates. These are restricted-support epigraph results; no reduction of arbitrary convex supports to these families is asserted.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The finite-table estimate and attained levels are used from 0cd230a98ae241c3 with map (4). Only the potential-independent scalar height calculation is used from dbcf5be1e541e0cf, with its translated height law mapped before (6). The compact positivity, four-site core coefficient, and single-coordinate estimates are used from a764225201e4e7d7 with the explicit maps (2), (3), and (11)-(14); the heterogeneous product argument is proved here. The selected-group boundary mass comparison is used from 3e20ef99e716d1db with its residual-cap map in (10). The Boolean core extension 6fe9007fe1ba4c4b is used with the original-law maps in (7) and the final corollary.
proof:
Replacing a real cap by its integer part leaves (1) unchanged. We therefore use \(T=\lfloor T\rfloor\) throughout the proof. The original support contains \((\mathbf0,0)\), so \(0<Z<\infty\). For \(T=0\), it is a singleton and \(M_3(p)=1\). All coefficients in (3) are at most one, so this case is settled. Henceforth \(T\ge1\).

Permuting spatial coordinates is an invertible affine map that bijects containing ambient halfspaces and preserves every original mass and depth. Relabel the groups so that
\(m=|I_1|\ge\ell=|I_2|\ge1\), hence \(k=m+\ell\le2m\). Write \(B_\star=B_1\) for the selected group's second cost and \(B_\circ=B_2\) for the other group's second cost.

We first establish the original-table consumers and two mass comparisons. Put \(r=e^{-\beta}\), \(f_E=\sum_{t=E}^T r^t\) for integers \(0\le E\le T\), and \(f_E=0\) for \(E>T\). Define \(a_{\mathbf x}=f_{\Gamma(\mathbf x)}\) on the spatial box, and zero outside it. The precise map to the finite table of accepted 0cd230a98ae241c3 is
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_a&=\lbrace\mathbf x:a_{\mathbf x}>0\rbrace,\qquad
 M_a=Z,\qquad a_{\max}=f_0,\\
A^a_\omega&=\lbrace\mathbf x:a_{\mathbf x}\ge\omega\rbrace,\qquad
r^a_\omega(\mathbf q)=|A^a_\omega\cap(2\mathbf q-A^a_\omega)|,\\
E(a)&=\sum_{\mathbf q\in D_a}
 \max_{0<\omega\le a_{\mathbf q}}\omega^4r^a_\omega(\mathbf q)^3,
\qquad
\chi(a)=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf x\in D_a}
 a_{\mathbf x}\log\frac{f_0}{a_{\mathbf x}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$
The interpolated slopes of \(g_i\) are
\(1,B_j-1,C_{4,i}-B_j\) when \(i\in I_j\), so they are nonnegative and nondecreasing. Thus each positive weak level of \(a\), being an energy sublevel of \(\Gamma\), is integer-midpoint-closed. The tail profile is strictly decreasing on its positive indices, and direct multiplication gives
\(f_E^2-f_{E-1}f_{E+1}=r^{E+T}>0\) for \(1\le E<T\), including \(r=1\). In particular it is logconcave. The attained-level assertion and finite-table bound of 0cd230a98ae241c3, under exactly (4), give
$$
E(a)\ge\frac{512}{19683(1+\chi(a))^3}\,8^{-k}Z^4.
\tag{5}
$$

The potential-independent original-height calculation of accepted dbcf5be1e541e0cf, (45)-(46), says that for the geometric law \(q_j=r^j/\sum_{i=0}^b r^i\) on \(\lbrace0,\ldots,b\rbrace\), extended by zero,
\(\sum_jq_j(\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}\min(q_{j+h},q_{j-h}))^3\ge1/448\).
Here \(b\) denotes only the integer length of this height interval. To check its use with our heterogeneous spatial potentials, fix a spatial root \(\mathbf q\) and a level \(f_E\le a_{\mathbf q}\), with \(R=r^a_{f_E}(\mathbf q)\). For \(E\le t\le T\), reflect spatial displacements in that level and height displacements \(|h|\le\min(t-E,T-t)\) about \((\mathbf q,t)\). Both endpoints are original atoms. The displacement involution has disjoint nonfixed pairs and the unique fixed zero displacement. Every closed halfspace through or containing the root contains an endpoint of each pair, and the smaller endpoint mass is \(r^{t+|h|}/Z\). Charging half the fixed root mass gives depth at least
$$
\frac R{2Z}\sum_{|h|\le\min(t-E,T-t)}r^{t+|h|}.
$$
The exact map to the accepted scalar height law is
\(b=T-E\), \(j=t-E\), and \(q_j=r^t/f_E\).
Cubing this lower bound and summing against the original root masses \(r^t/Z\) gives \(R^3f_E^4/(3584Z^4)\).
At every spatial root choose one attaining level, available by 0cd230a98ae241c3, and sum over distinct roots. This proves
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac{E(a)}{3584Z^4}.
\tag{6}
$$
This argument, rather than a common-second-cost hypothesis, is what justifies the height consumer here.

For a spread bound, let \(\phi\) be the convex nondecreasing linear interpolation of \(-\log(f_E/f_0)\), with \(\phi(0)=0\). Coordinatewise rounding \(F(\mathbf x)_i=\lfloor x_i/2\rfloor\) satisfies \(g_i(F(\mathbf x)_i)\le g_i(x_i)/2\): its only nonzero checks are \(1\le B_j/2\) and \(1\le C_{4,i}/2\). Consequently \(\phi(\Gamma(F(\mathbf x)))\le\phi(\Gamma(\mathbf x))/2\). Each image has at most \(2^k\) preimages. For the auxiliary normalized table \(\widetilde a_{\mathbf x}=a_{\mathbf x}/f_0\), Jensen under its full spatial probability law gives
$$
e^{\chi(a)/2}
 \le\frac{\sum_{\mathbf x}\sqrt{\widetilde a_{\mathbf x}}}
          {\sum_{\mathbf x}\widetilde a_{\mathbf x}}
 \le2^k\le3^k.
$$
Thus \(\chi(a)\le2k\log3\). If \(m<N_{\rm two}\), then \(k<2N_{\rm two}\), and (5)-(6) prove the theorem with \(\kappa_{\rm small}\) in (3). We henceforth assume \(m\ge N_{\rm two}\).

For \(b=2,3\), let \(Z_{\star,b}\) be the portion of the original \(Z\) in which all selected coordinates lie in \(\lbrace0,\ldots,b-1\rbrace\), and let \(p_{\star,b}\) be its normalized law in the same ambient space. We claim
$$
M_3(p_{\star,2})\ge\kappa_{\rm mix}8^{-(k+1)},
\qquad
M_3(p_{\star,3})\ge\kappa_{\rm mix}8^{-(k+1)}.
\tag{7}
$$
For \(b=3\), the exact map to the application of accepted 6fe9007fe1ba4c4b is: its four-site core rank is \(\ell\); its common second cost is \(B_\circ\); its core fourth costs are the present \(C_{4,i}\) for \(i\in I_2\); its adjoined number of coordinates is \(m\), each with second cost \(B_\star\); its cap and tilt are our \(T,\beta\); and its original normalizer is \(Z_{\star,3}\). Its four-site coefficient from a764225201e4e7d7 is precisely the \(\kappa_{\rm four}\) in (3). For \(b=2\), make the same map except that every adjoined second cost is the artificial integer \(T+1\ge2\). These artificial third sites are infeasible under the cap, so that law is exactly \(p_{\star,2}\), including its ambient coordinates, normalizer, and depths. This proves both claims. For either law, every original containing-halfspace mass and every sampled atom mass in its support are at least \(Z_{\star,b}/Z\) times their values in that law. Therefore
$$
M_3(p)\ge (Z_{\star,b}/Z)^4M_3(p_{\star,b}).
\tag{8}
$$

Fix disjoint subsets of selected coordinates at sites 2 and 3, and let their fixed energy be \(E_{\rm fix}\). Shifting the height by \(E_{\rm fix}\) expresses that sector's full mass as \(e^{-\beta E_{\rm fix}}\) times the mass of the remaining binary selected coordinates and the unchanged other group, capped at \(T-E_{\rm fix}\). Appending zeros in the removed selected coordinates embeds the shifted support into the support for \(Z_{\star,2}\). If \(T-E_{\rm fix}<0\) the sector is empty. Summing these sector bounds gives
$$
Z\le Z_{\star,2}
 \prod_{i\in I_1}(1+e^{-\beta B_\star}+e^{-\beta C_{4,i}})
 \le Z_{\star,2}(1+2e^{-\beta B_\star})^m.
\tag{9}
$$
If \(\beta B_\star\ge\log m\), this ratio is at most \(e^2\), and (7)-(8) settle the theorem with coefficient \(e^{-8}\kappa_{\rm mix}\). Henceforth
\(\beta B_\star<\log m\).

For every real \(A\ge0\), we also have
$$
\frac{T}{B_\star}\le A\sqrt m
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{Z}{Z_{\star,3}}\le e^{256A^2},
\qquad
M_3(p)\ge\kappa_{\rm mix}e^{-1024A^2}8^{-(k+1)}.
\tag{10}
$$
Indeed, fix one other-group spatial vector of energy \(E_\circ\le T\), and shift its energy out of the height. Its residual cap is the integer \(U=T-E_\circ\). The selected four-site mass at cap \(U\), multiplied by \(e^{-\beta E_\circ}\), is exactly that vector's original slice mass. By support inclusion it is at most the selected homogeneous boundary mass with costs \((0,1,B_\star,2B_\star-1)\), cap \(U\), and the same tilt. Its complete selected three-site mass is unchanged. The exact map to (2) of accepted 3e20ef99e716d1db is its rank \(k=m\), cost \(B=B_\star\), cap \(T=U\), tilt equal to ours, and \(R=\lfloor U/B_\star\rfloor\le A\sqrt m\). Thus its ratio is at most \(e^{256A^2}\). Summing over the other spatial vectors with the same positive factors \(e^{-\beta E_\circ}\) proves the mass assertion in (10). Its moment assertion is (7)-(8). No bound with total rank in place of selected rank was used.

We next construct the product saddle. For \(i\in I_j\), retain the canonical scalar variables
\(u=s\), \(v_j=sB_j\), \(\xi=e^{-u}\), \(\eta_j=e^{-v_j}\), and \(\zeta_i=e^{-sC_{4,i}}\). Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
I_\lambda&=\lbrace h\in\mathbb Z:\lambda+h,\lambda-h\in
 \lbrace0,1,2,3\rbrace\rbrace,\\
e_{i,\lambda}(h)&=
 \tfrac12[g_i(\lambda+h)+g_i(\lambda-h)]-g_i(\lambda),\\
b_{i,\lambda}(h)&=
 \tfrac12[g_i(\lambda+h)-g_i(\lambda-h)],\\
K_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\sum_{h\in I_\lambda}
 e^{-(2s/3)[g_i(\lambda+h)+g_i(\lambda-h)]},\\
H_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\sum_{h\in I_\lambda}
 e^{-(4s/3)e_{i,\lambda}(h)},\\
Z_i(s)&=1+\xi+\eta_j+\zeta_i,\qquad
P_i(s)=\sum_{\lambda=0}^3K_{s,i}(\lambda)^3,\\
\delta_i(s)&=\log\frac{8P_i(s)}{Z_i(s)^4},
\qquad Q_{s,i}(\lambda)=K_{s,i}(\lambda)^3/P_i(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
$$
The symbol \(b_{i,\lambda}(h)\) denotes only the imbalance. Let \(J_i\) have law \(Q_{s,i}\), and conditionally on \(J_i=\lambda\), let its displacement \(V_i\) have probabilities \(e^{-(4s/3)e_{i,\lambda}(h)}/H_{s,i}(\lambda)\). The excess is nonnegative, and conditional imbalance has mean zero by \(h\mapsto-h\). Set
$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar e_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\mathbb E[e_{i,\lambda}(V_i)\mid J_i=\lambda],\\
\sigma^e_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\mathbb E[e_{i,\lambda}(V_i)^2\mid J_i=\lambda],\\
\sigma^b_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\mathbb E[b_{i,\lambda}(V_i)^2\mid J_i=\lambda],\\
\alpha_{s,i}(\lambda)&=g_i(\lambda)+\bar e_{s,i}(\lambda),
\qquad \mu_i(s)=\mathbb E\alpha_{s,i}(J_i),\\
R_i(s)&=s^2\left(1+\mathbb E[
 g_i(J_i)^2+e_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2+b_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2]\right),\\
\mu(s)&=\sum_i\mu_i(s),\qquad V_s=\sum_iR_i(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$
Here \(\sigma^b\) is the conditional imbalance variance; \(\sigma^e\) is its excess second-moment counterpart. This single consistent convention replaces the two labels \(v^\eta\) in (30)-(31) and \(v^b\) in the coordinate-index convention of a764225201e4e7d7.

We import only the one-coordinate scalar estimates proved in (18)-(32) of that accepted fact, with the following exact map separately for each \(i\in I_j\): its \(g,B,C_4,s,u,v,w,\xi,\eta,\zeta\) are the present
\(g_i,B_j,C_{4,i},s,u,v_j,sC_{4,i},\xi,\eta_j,\zeta_i\);
its \(Z_g,P_g,\delta_g,\mathcal R_g,\mu_g\) are \(Z_i,P_i,\delta_i,R_i,\mu_i\); and its conditional excess, imbalance, root law, displacement law, and \(\alpha\) are exactly (11)-(12). These assertions each concern one coordinate with arbitrary \(B\ge2\) and \(C_4\ge2B-1\). Thus their hypotheses hold individually; no common \(B\) is being claimed for a product. The estimates are
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\delta_i(s)\ge0\quad(s\ge0),\\
&\delta_i(s)\ge\varepsilon
 \quad\text{if }s\ge1\text{, or if }0\le s\le1,\ v_j\le24,\\
&0<R_i(s)<256
 \quad(0<s\le s_{\max}:=12\log2),\\
&s^2\mathbb E\alpha_{s,i}(J_i)^2\le2R_i(s),\qquad
 s^2\mathbb E[\sigma^e_{s,i}(J_i)+\sigma^b_{s,i}(J_i)]\le R_i(s),\\
&\frac14(\log P_i)'(s)=-\mu_i(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
$$
When \(0<s\le1\) and \(v_j\ge24\), with \(q_j=e^{-2v_j/3}\), the sharper estimates are
$$
\delta_i(s)\ge(u^2+q_j)/1024,\qquad
R_i(s)\le2u^2+128v_j^2q_j,\qquad
\mu_i(s)/B_j\le1/B_j+64q_j.
\tag{14}
$$
In particular (13) and Cauchy-Schwarz imply \(s\mu_i(s)<32\) for \(0<s\le s_{\max}\).
The finite 56-tuple expansion underlying (13) also has exactly one zero-energy tuple and all other tuple energies at least 4, since \(g_i(1)=1\) and all higher-site costs are at least 2. This last observation holds for every present coordinate.

For precision, we now reprove the product saddle and concentration argument with these possibly different scalar costs. Let
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(s)&=\max_{0\le t\le T,\ t\in\mathbb Z}
 [\log(f_t/f_0)+st],\\
\mathcal J(s)&=\lbrace t:\log(f_t/f_0)+st=\mathcal F(s)\rbrace,\\
L(s)&=40\sqrt{\sum_i\left(1+\mathbb E[
 g_i(J_i)^2+e_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2+b_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2]\right)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
$$
The exact finite-sum expectations make \(L\) continuous on \([0,s_{\max}]\); for \(s>0\), \(L(s)=40\sqrt{V_s}/s\). Minimize the continuous function
\(\Psi(s)=\mathcal F(s)+\tfrac14\sum_i\log P_i(s)-\int_0^sL(y)\,dy\)
on this compact interval. At zero, \(\mathcal F\) has unique active index zero because \(f_t<f_0\) for \(t>0\). Its right derivative is zero, so (13) gives
\(\Psi'_+(0)=-\mu(0)-L(0)<0\). The minimizing rate is positive.

The maximum defining \(\mathcal F\) gives the original-mass bound
$$
Z\le f_0e^{\mathcal F(s)}\prod_i Z_i(s)
 =f_t e^{st}\prod_i Z_i(s)\qquad(t\in\mathcal J(s)).
\tag{16}
$$
This follows pointwise at every feasible spatial vector by using \(t=\Gamma(\mathbf x)\) in that maximum, then summing over the full spatial box.

At an interior minimum, the left and right derivatives of \(\mathcal F\) are the smallest and largest active integer indices. By (13) they bracket \(\mu(s)+L(s)\). Logconcavity of \(f_t\) makes these active indices consecutive. Hence there is an active integer \(t_\star\) with
$$
\mu(s)+40\sqrt{V_s}/s\le t_\star
 \le\mu(s)+40\sqrt{V_s}/s+1.
\tag{17}
$$
If the minimum is at \(s=s_{\max}\), choose its smallest active integer instead. The nonpositive left derivative then gives
\(t_\star\le\mu(s)+40\sqrt{V_s}/s\).

At an interior minimum, sample the roots independently with laws \(Q_{s,i}\).
Call a root \(\boldsymbol\lambda\) good if
$$
\left|s\sum_i\alpha_{s,i}(\lambda_i)-s\mu(s)\right|
 \le8\sqrt{V_s},
\qquad
s^2\sum_i[\sigma^e_{s,i}(\lambda_i)+\sigma^b_{s,i}(\lambda_i)]
 \le64V_s.
\tag{18}
$$
Independence and (13), Chebyshev, Markov, and a union bound give probability at least \(1-3/64>1/2\).
For a fixed good root, conditionally independent displacements satisfy, with probability at least \(3/4\),
$$
\left|s\sum_i[e_{i,\lambda_i}(V_i)-\bar e_{s,i}(\lambda_i)]\right|
 \le16\sqrt{V_s},
\qquad
\left|s\sum_i b_{i,\lambda_i}(V_i)\right|\le16\sqrt{V_s}.
\tag{19}
$$
Indeed the sum of their two failure bounds is at most \(64/256=1/4\). Independence between excess and imbalance in the same coordinate is unnecessary.
The exact endpoint identity is
\(\Gamma(\boldsymbol\lambda\pm\mathbf h)=
\Gamma(\boldsymbol\lambda)+\sum_i e_{i,\lambda_i}(h_i)
 \pm\sum_i b_{i,\lambda_i}(h_i)\).
Equations (17)-(19) put both endpoints, and the root itself, in the original energy sublevel at \(t_\star\).

Reciprocal conditional density on the event (19), using its lower excess bound, gives at least
$$
\frac12\prod_iH_{s,i}(\lambda_i)
 \exp\left(\frac{4s}{3}\sum_i\bar e_{s,i}(\lambda_i)
                 -\frac{64}{3}\sqrt{V_s}\right)
$$
distinct displacements there. The endpoint map is injective, so this lower bounds \(r^a_{f_{t_\star}}(\boldsymbol\lambda)\).
The exact product identity
\(\prod_iH_{s,i}(\lambda_i)^3=
e^{4s\Gamma(\boldsymbol\lambda)}(\prod_iP_i(s))
\prod_iQ_{s,i}(\lambda_i)\)
uses each coordinate's own kernel. Cube the count, sum over good roots, and use the lower side of (18) and good-root probability at least \(1/2\). It follows that
$$
E(a)\ge\frac1{16}f_{t_\star}^4
 \left(\prod_iP_i(s)\right)
 \exp(4s\mu(s)-96\sqrt{V_s}).
$$
Division by (16) to the fourth power and (17) prove
$$
\frac{E(a)}{Z^4}\ge\frac1{16}
 \exp\left(\sum_i\delta_i(s)-256\sqrt{V_s}-4s\right)8^{-k}.
\tag{20}
$$
Every estimate in this product derivation used scalar identities (13) with sums or products over coordinates; a common second cost was never used.

The endpoint alternative is settled uniformly as follows. The tuple observation after (14), with exactly 56 tuples, gives
\(P_i(s/2)-1\le55e^{-2s}\).
For any positive tuple energy \(\Xi\),
\((s\Xi)e^{-s\Xi}\le(2/e)e^{-s\Xi/2}\).
The derivative identity gives \(s\mu_i(s)<1/4\) at \(s=s_{\max}\), since \(55\cdot2^{-24}<1\).
Also \(Z_i(s)\le1+2^{-12}+2^{-24}+2^{-36}\), so \(\log Z_i(s)<1/16\).
The endpoint inequality for \(t_\star\), (13), (16), and \(f_{t_\star}\le f_0\) imply
$$
\log(Z/f_0)\le5k/16+40\sqrt{V_s}
 <5k/16+640\sqrt k.
$$
The original spatial zero root has its self-reflection at level \(f_0\), hence \(E(a)\ge f_0^4\).
As \(k\ge m\ge N_{\rm two}\ge2^{1024}\), we have
\(2560\sqrt k\le k/4\). Thus
\(E(a)/Z^4\ge e^{-3k/2}\ge8^{-k}\), using \(\log2>1/2\).
Equation (6) settles this alternative with coefficient \(1/448\), larger than the coefficient in (3).

For an interior rate, (13) gives \(V_s<256k\le512m\). If \(s\ge1\), or if \(s\le1\) and the selected \(v=v_1=sB_\star\le24\), the selected group contributes at least \(m\varepsilon\) to \(\sum_i\delta_i\), while all other terms are nonnegative. By (3),
\(m\varepsilon\ge2^{16}\sqrt m>256\sqrt{512m}+48\).
This dominates \(256\sqrt{V_s}+4s\). Equation (20) gives \(E(a)/Z^4\ge8^{-k}/16\), and (6) gives the coefficient \(1/7168\).
The same conclusion holds whenever
\(\sum_i\delta_i(s)\ge256\sqrt{V_s}+4s\).

It remains to examine an interior bad saddle with
$$
0<u=s\le1,\qquad v=sB_\star\ge24,\qquad
\sum_i\delta_i(s)<256\sqrt{V_s}+4s.
\tag{21}
$$
Put \(q=e^{-2v/3}\), \(U=mu^2\), \(Q=mq\), \(G=U+Q\), and set \(A_{\rm aux}=2^{19}\).
Since \(V_s\ge ks^2\ge s^2\), the right side of (21) is at most \(260\sqrt{V_s}\).
The selected lower bound (14) alone is \(G/1024\).
We prove, in all possible positions of the other scale, that
$$
G\le K_{\rm two}v^2,
\qquad
t_\star/B_\star\le H_{\rm two}\sqrt m.
\tag{22}
$$
The following three cases exhaust the other scale. We give the global bounds and all mean comparisons explicitly.

First suppose \(B_\circ\ge B_\star\). Write \(v_\circ=sB_\circ\ge v\).
Both \(x^2e^{-2x/3}\) and \(xe^{-2x/3}\) decrease on \([24,\infty)\).
Using \(\ell\le m\) in (14) therefore gives
$$
V_s\le4U+256v^2Q,\qquad
\mu(s)/B_\star\le2m/B_\star+128Q.
\tag{23}
$$
For the mean inequality, an other-coordinate contribution divided by \(B_\star\) is at most
\(1/B_\star+64(v_\circ/v)e^{-2v_\circ/3}
 \le1/B_\star+64q\).
The selected surplus and (21) give
\(G<A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_s}\).
Squaring (23), and using \(U,Q\le G\), yields
\(G<A_{\rm aux}^2(4+256v^2)<2^{47}v^2\le K_{\rm two}v^2\).
Consequently
$$
m/B_\star=\sqrt m\,\sqrt U/v\le\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}\sqrt m,
\qquad
Q=\sqrt m\,\sqrt Q\,e^{-v/3}
 \le2\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}\sqrt m,
\tag{24}
$$
where \(ve^{-v/3}\le3/e<2\).
Furthermore the global radius and \(v\ge24\) give
\(\sqrt{V_s}/v<\sqrt m\), because \(512<24^2\).
Equation (17), (23), and (24) imply
$$
t_\star/B_\star
 \le(258\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}+41)\sqrt m
 \le H_{\rm two}\sqrt m.
$$
Here the rounding term \(1/B_\star\le1/2\) was bounded by \(\sqrt m\).
This proves (22) in the first case.

Second suppose \(B_\circ\le B_\star\) and \(v_\circ=sB_\circ\ge24\).
Define
$$
U_{\rm all}=ku^2,\qquad
Q_{\rm all}=mq+\ell e^{-2v_\circ/3},\qquad
G_{\rm all}=U_{\rm all}+Q_{\rm all}.
$$
All coordinates obey (14), so
\(\sum_i\delta_i\ge G_{\rm all}/1024\) and
\(V_s\le2U_{\rm all}+128v^2Q_{\rm all}\).
Failure (21) gives
\(G_{\rm all}<A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_s}\), hence
\(G_{\rm all}<A_{\rm aux}^2(2+128v^2)<2^{46}v^2\).
In particular \(G\le G_{\rm all}\le K_{\rm two}v^2\).
The global radius also gives
\(Q_{\rm all}\le G_{\rm all}<2^{24}\sqrt m\).
The mean inequality (14), after multiplication by each group's \(B_j/B_\star\le1\), yields
$$
\mu(s)/B_\star\le k/B_\star+64Q_{\rm all},\qquad
k/B_\star=\sqrt k\,\sqrt{U_{\rm all}}/v
 \le2\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}\sqrt m.
$$
Since \(K_{\rm two}\ge2^{50}\), it follows that
\(\mu(s)/B_\star\le66\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}\sqrt m\).
Again \(\sqrt{V_s}/v<\sqrt m\), so (17) proves (22) with the stated \(H_{\rm two}\).

Third suppose \(v_\circ=sB_\circ\le24\).
The other group contributes at least \(\varepsilon\ell\) by (13).
Set \(F=G+D_\varepsilon\ell\) and \(V_0=2U+128v^2Q\).
Then
$$
\sum_i\delta_i\ge F/1024,\qquad
V_s\le V_0+256\ell,\qquad
F<A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_0+256\ell}.
$$
Since \(\ell\le F/D_\varepsilon\), taking square roots termwise gives
$$
F<A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_0}
 +16A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{F/D_\varepsilon}
 \le A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_0}+\frac F2+
       \frac{128A_{\rm aux}^2}{D_\varepsilon}.
$$
Consequently
$$
F<2A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{V_0}+K_0,
\qquad K_0=\frac{256A_{\rm aux}^2}{D_\varepsilon}
         =\frac{2^{46}}{D_\varepsilon}.
\tag{25}
$$
As \(V_0\le(2+128v^2)G\) and
\(2A_{\rm aux}\sqrt{2+128v^2}<32A_{\rm aux}v\),
another application of \(ab\le(a^2+b^2)/2\) gives

 \le G/2+512A_{\rm aux}^2v^2+K_0,
$$
so
\(G<(2^{48}+2K_0)v^2\le K_{\rm two}v^2\).
Here \(v^2\ge1\) was used to absorb \(2K_0\).
Also \(\sup_{x\ge0}x^2e^{-2x/3}=9/e^2<9\), and \(u\le1\), so
\(V_0<1154m<2048m\).
Equation (25) and \(m\ge1\) show
$$
\ell<\left(\frac{2^{26}}{D_\varepsilon}
          +\frac{2^{46}}{D_\varepsilon^2}\right)\sqrt m
 \le K_{\rm two}\sqrt m.
\tag{26}
$$
The selected mean bound, exactly as in (24), is
\(\mu_\star(s)/B_\star\le129\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}\sqrt m\).
For the other mean, use \(s\mu_i(s)<32\) from (13), obtaining
\(\mu_\circ(s)/B_\star<32\ell/v\le2\ell
 \le2K_{\rm two}\sqrt m\).
Finally \(\sqrt{V_s}/v<\sqrt m\), and (17) gives

t_\star/B_\star
 \le(129\sqrt{K_{\rm two}}+2K_{\rm two}+41)\sqrt m

This proves (22) in the third case. Every absorption above follows from

If \(T/B_\star\le2H_{\rm two}\sqrt m\), apply (10) with \(A=2H_{\rm two}\). This proves the theorem with coefficient

Otherwise \(T/B_\star>2H_{\rm two}\sqrt m\). By (22), \(t_\star<T/2<T\).
Compare its active value in (15) with that at the forward neighbor. This gives

s\le\log(f_{t_\star}/f_{t_\star+1})
 \le\beta+\frac1{T-t_\star}\le\beta+\frac2T.

For the middle bound, with \(b=T-t_\star\ge1\), the tail ratio is

Using \(\beta B_\star<\log m\) and \(H_{\rm two}\sqrt m\ge1\), we obtain

Q=me^{-2v/3}>e^{-2/3}m^{1/3}.

But (22) gives \(Q\le K_{\rm two}(\log m+1)^2\), contradicting the cutoff in (3).
Here is an explicit check with no asymptotic assertion. Write \(L=\log m\ge1024K_{\rm two}\).

Thus (27) and the upper bound for \(Q\) cannot hold. The remaining large-cap bad-saddle case is empty.

We have covered bounded selected rank, both original-mass transfer branches, the endpoint saddle, the surplus-paying interior saddle, and every other interior saddle.
